column1: # CLAIMS.tsv -- every number this site states about the toolchain, and the
# command that printed it.
#   npm run claims          # the cheap rows -- seconds
#   npm run claims:all      # also the real gates, in the sibling checkouts
#   npm run claims:sweep    # numbers on the swept pages with no row here
# WHY THIS LIVES HERE, of all places. This is where the worst instance happened.
# The site said aowlsem was "498/498 byte-exact modules with the entire
# std/system checking clean". 498 was never a module count: it is
# aowlsem/REQUIREMENTS.md's hconv-SITE census -- "all 54 modules | oracle 527 |
# ours 498" -- reworded. The real module figure that day was 46/55. It stood for
# weeks, on the page a reader trusts most, and nothing could catch it because no
# test reads prose.
# It is also the only place in the toolchain that makes CROSS-REPO claims: these
# pages quote aowlsem's gates, aowlc's, aowli's, aowlparser's, aowlhexer's and
# aowlmony's. A number is furthest from its gate exactly here, which is why the
# SOURCE column of most rows is `cd ~/<repo> && <its gate>`. The gate lives in
# the repo, the claim lives here, and this file is the wire between them.
# THE CHEAP ROWS ARE DENOMINATORS AND VERSIONS, deliberately. Every defect this
# toolchain has had was one of the two drifting: aowlc's corpus grew 77 -> 78 and
# its README did not follow; aowlsem's grew past the 31 its README quoted; and
# aowli's release reads v0.3.5 on aowli.md, v0.3.3 on blog.md, v0.3.2 and v0.3.1
# on the release page, while `git tag` in aowli says v0.3.2 is the newest. A
# numerator costs a corpus run. A denominator is `ls` and a version is `git tag`.
# WHAT IT WILL NOT DO. It never rewrites a number. When a gate disagrees it
# prints what the gate said and stops, because pasting an unmeasured figure is
# the original defect. It also refuses to read a REFUSED gate as a
# disagreement: aowlsem's idxchecksum.sh exits 2 with "the ARTIFACTS are stale",
# aowli's lanes print "THIS RUN IS NOT EVIDENCE", aowlparser's stress.sh answers
# `pass=0 ... oracle-skip=225` when its nifler oracle is absent. Those rows carry
# GUARD regexes and come back UNVERIFIABLE. A zero that means "no oracle" read as
# a measurement is exactly how a confident wrong correction gets written.
# PLATFORM rows are never run. aowlsem's moddiff.baseline is a LINUX measurement
# and this box is Windows; module ids are content-hashed and the trees differ, so
# the module SETS differ. The two numbers are not two readings of one thing.
# UNATTRIBUTED rows fail the run on purpose -- no command produces them at all.
# That is the 498/498 class, and the fix for one is to measure it or delete it,
# never to write something that sounds right. Seven are listed today; each note
# carries the command that would settle it. They are the ranked debt.
# ONE ENVIRONMENT NOTE, because it is the difference between a green run and a
# confidently wrong one: put /c/msys64/ucrt64/bin FIRST in PATH before
# `npm run claims`. Without it msys2's cc1.exe exits 127 with no output, aowlc's
# npm test answers `0/24 passed`, and a checker without the `gcc failed` guard
# would call 21/24 wrong. It is guarded, so it reports UNVERIFIABLE instead --
# but the guarded answer is not a measurement either.
# Columns: FILE <TAB> ANCHOR <TAB> CLASS <TAB> NUMBER <TAB> SOURCE <TAB> EXTRACT <TAB> GUARD

column1: # Jester (savannt/jester, private) is a sibling checkout like the rest: its gates
# run in ~/Documents/infiniteless-next. The two counts below are the spine of that
# section -- "the boundary is N host calls" is the claim the whole design rests on,
# and it moved once already: HOST-SURFACE.md's 205 was measured before the content-
# update table (15 calls) existed, and the site said 220 from the first day because
# these rows were run rather than remembered. The GUARD on each is the missing-
# checkout case: with no jester tree the greps print nothing and 0 would otherwise
# read as a measurement.
# AND THEN IT DRIFTED ANYWAY, 220 -> 433, because these rows were not run for
# months and nothing else read the prose. Two changes came out of that. First,
# the host-call command no longer names the prefix-owned families: it reads the
# family list out of the bridge's own `XHostCalls.Prefix` references, so a family
# nobody told it about is counted the day it is added -- which is exactly how the
# old command went wrong, by hard-coding four families while eleven grew. Second,
# the per-family breakdown table on docs/jester/host-surface.md is no longer
# typed at all: `node tools/jester-surface.mjs ~/Documents/infiniteless-next
# --write` regenerates it between its markers, and refuses to print anything
# while any call falls outside its area map. The rows below gate the generated
# totals, so a stale block is a failing row rather than a quiet lie.
docs/jester.md
column5: cd ~/Documents/infiniteless-next && P=Packages/com.infiniteless.runtime/Runtime; { grep -ohE 'case "infiniteless_[a-z0-9_]+"' $P/Native/AowliHostBridge.cs | grep -oE 'infiniteless_[a-z0-9_]+'; for c in $(grep -ohE '[A-Za-z]+HostCalls\.Prefix' $P/Native/AowliHostBridge.cs | sed 's/\.Prefix//' | sort -u); do f=$(find $P -name "$c.cs"); q=$(grep -ohE 'Prefix = "infiniteless_[a-z0-9_]+"' $f | grep -oE 'infiniteless_[a-z0-9_]+'); grep -ohE 'case Prefix \+ "[a-z0-9_]+"' $f | grep -oE '"[a-z0-9_]+"$' | tr -d '"' | sed "s|^|$q|"; done; } | sort -u | wc -l | sed 's/ //g;s/^/host-calls=/'
